clue.text: Shut up, being intimidated outwardly, in the byre

indicators.note: something acting outwardly wraps around the outside, so one word encloses the other

blocks.note: cowed means intimidated into submission
sh! is what you say to tell someone to shut up

explanation.surface: A frightened animal hushed and cowering in its byre.
explanation.walkthrough: A byre is a cowshed, an old word still used in Scotland and northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: A byre is a farm building where cattle are housed, which is exactly a shed for cows.

clue.text: Enticed and inveigled by rotter, pretty one's gone missing

indicators.note: something gone missing is absent, so a letter is dropped
to be inveigled by someone is to be drawn into their grasp, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a cad is a rotter, a dishonourable man
jolie is French for pretty
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A pretty young woman lured and seduced by a scoundrel, then gone.
explanation.walkthrough: Pretty is taken in French here, a common Araucaria trick; the one that goes missing is the Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: To cajole is to persuade by flattery or coaxing, so cajoled means lured or tempted.

clue.text: Indications this month I deplore in the Guardian that gave PM a hard time

definitions.text: that gave PM a hard time

indicators.note: in places the preceding pieces inside the following word

blocks.note: the newspaper speaks in its leaders as the editorial we
omens are signs or indications
inst. is the commercial abbreviation for this month
taken as written
tut is the noise of disapproval

explanation.surface: A Guardian reader deploring this month's signs, about a group that heckled the Prime Minister.
explanation.walkthrough: In June 2000 the Women's Institute slow-handclapped Tony Blair at its conference. The Guardian's editorial voice is WE, which wraps the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: The Women's Institute, a British women's organisation, famously heckled Prime Minister Tony Blair at its 2000 conference.

clue.text: A minimum of work on the clock?

definitions.text: A minimum of work on the clock?

blocks.note: the surface reading: the least possible effort, the idiom for doing nothing at all when used in the negative
the setter's reading: what the pointers on a clock face do as time passes

explanation.walkthrough: Not doing a hand's turn means not lifting a finger; read literally, a clock's hands do turn.
explanation.definitionFit: A hand's turn is a stroke of work, the smallest amount of effort, and clock hands literally turn.

clue.text: On being taken from the keep I am placed in mustard city

indicators.note: taken from means removed out of, so letters disappear
placed means put into position inside what remains

blocks.note: a donjon is the keep, or great tower, of a castle
taken as written, to be removed
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone moved out of a castle keep and resettled in a mustard city.
explanation.walkthrough: Keep looks like a verb, but it is the noun for a castle's main tower. Only the first ON comes out, leaving one in the second half.
explanation.definitionFit: Dijon in Burgundy is the French city famous for its mustard, which bears the city's name.

clue.text: Comparatively cheeky hand

blocks.note: first meaning: more flip, flip being slang for impertinent
second meaning: a slang word for a person's hand

explanation.walkthrough: The comparative of flip (glib, impertinent) adds -PER; the same word is old slang for a hand, as in 'give us your flipper'.
explanation.definitionFit: Flip means impertinent, so its comparative is more impertinent; flipper is also jocular slang for a human hand.

clue.text: Earnest acknowledgment among the trees at the end

indicators.note: among puts one piece in the midst of another
end points to the final letter of the word before it

blocks.note: a forest is a mass of trees
ta is British informal for thank you
last letter of the

explanation.surface: A serious thank-you given among the trees at the end of a walk.
explanation.walkthrough: Earnest looks like an adjective for serious; here it is the noun for a token or pledge of what is to come.
explanation.definitionFit: An earnest is a token payment or sign of more to follow, which is a taste in advance of the whole.

clue.text: Setter's got his set - buzz off!

indicators.note: to set something is to arrange it, so the letters are placed in a new order

blocks.note: the setter refers to himself as I, so the setter is I'M
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: The setter has assembled his kit and is told to clear off.
explanation.walkthrough: Imshi is old British army slang, from Arabic, for go away.
explanation.definitionFit: Imshi is a slang command meaning go away, picked up by soldiers in the Middle East, so it equals scram.

clue.text: I accept help with soil management, which 2 didn't like

indicators.note: managing things means arranging them, so the letters are organised afresh

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gardener gladly accepting help with the earth, which the Women's Institute disliked.
explanation.walkthrough: 2 is the Women's Institute, which heckled Tony Blair in 2000 for making a political speech at its conference.
explanation.definitionFit: The Women's Institute objected that Blair's address to them was partisan, a speech of party politics rather than a neutral talk.

clue.text: Stagger round defence ministry to change its structure

indicators.note: round means going about the outside, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: to reel is to stagger
MoD is the UK Ministry of Defence

explanation.surface: Reeling under a defence ministry reorganisation.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ministry of Defence is the British government department for the armed forces.
explanation.definitionFit: To remodel is to rework the form or shape of something, so it is to alter its structure.

clue.text: Marmalade's jejune, pointless, ridiculous - 2's trademarks

indicators.note: without a point means a compass point letter is dropped from the letters available
something ridiculous is absurdly out of order, so the remaining letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of both words, before one compass point is dropped

explanation.surface: A sneer at marmalade as feeble, pointless and absurd, like a cranky food review.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop one E (East, a point of the compass) and rearrange. 2 is the Women's Institute, whose image is summed up by jam-making and singing Blake's hymn Jerusalem.
explanation.definitionFit: Jam-making and the hymn Jerusalem sung at meetings are the stereotypical hallmarks associated with the Women's Institute.

clue.text: Golfing connections

definitions.note: adjective here; the answer is a noun for a golf course

blocks.note: first meaning: a seaside golf course
second meaning: things that join, like the loops of a chain

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as contacts made on the fairway; the first meaning is the golf course itself, the second the joins of a chain.
explanation.definitionFit: Links is the name for a coastal golf course, and links are also the joining rings of a chain.

clue.text: Ulster was a tease, being foolish

blocks.note: Northern Ireland, often called Ulster, abbreviated
to twit someone is to tease them, so twitted means teased

explanation.surface: Someone from Northern Ireland was a joker, acting silly.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitwitted describes behaving like a nitwit, a stupid person, so it is a synonym for silly or daft.

clue.text: Change for a quid at the "Flag" from drinks

indicators.note: to change something is to alter its form, so these letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
the yellow flag is a wild iris

explanation.surface: Getting change for a pound at a pub called the Flag.
explanation.walkthrough: A pub sign suggests the Flag is an inn; it is the plant, a flag being a kind of iris. A quid is British slang for a pound.
explanation.definitionFit: Daiquiris are rum cocktails made with lime juice and sugar, so they are a kind of drink.

clue.text: In reference to the drawer, I withdraw

blocks.note: re means concerning, with reference to
a tractor draws, that is pulls, loads

explanation.surface: Someone retracting a statement about the person who drew a picture.
explanation.walkthrough: The drawer suggests an artist or a cabinet drawer; here it is something that pulls. The answer then speaks of itself: a retractor is anything that withdraws.
explanation.definitionFit: A retractor is one who takes back a statement, or a surgical tool that holds back tissue, so it speaks as one that pulls back.

clue.text: His Grace's related to 2 (round number)

indicators.note: going round something encloses it, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: dual means relating to two
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: A duke's title somehow linked to clue 2, the Women's Institute.
explanation.walkthrough: 2 looks like a cross-reference to the Women's Institute, but here it is just the number two.
explanation.definitionFit: A duke is addressed as His Grace, and ducal is the adjective for anything belonging to a duke.

clue.text: The Lord's party, a small one, to call for curtailment

indicators.note: curtailing cuts off the tail, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: a do is a party
a mini is a small one of its kind
call, before its last letter is cut

explanation.surface: The Lord's party, a modest one, calling for cutbacks.
explanation.definitionFit: Dominical, from Latin dominus, means relating to the Lord, as in the dominical letter or the Lord's Day.

clue.text: Welles's "Golden Boy"

blocks.note: or is the heraldic word for gold
a son is a boy

explanation.surface: The title of an Orson Welles film or role, Golden Boy.
explanation.walkthrough: Golden Boy really is a play and film title, which hides the split into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The director and actor Welles was called Orson, so the first name is what belongs to him.

clue.text: Stuffed a complete American policeman

blocks.note: something over is finished, complete
a fed is a US federal agent

explanation.surface: Someone stuffed a whole American cop, as if into a sack.
explanation.definitionFit: Overfed means given too much to eat, so it matches stuffed in the sense of full after eating.

clue.text: The "Jolly Fellow" - how gliders ascend

blocks.note: taken as written
a jolly is slang for a Royal Marine
a fellow in arms is an ally

explanation.surface: A pub or ship called the Jolly Fellow, and how gliders climb.
explanation.walkthrough: Jolly is old naval slang for a Royal Marine, abbreviated RM.
explanation.definitionFit: Gliders gain height by circling in rising currents of warm air, so they climb by means of heat.

clue.text: British policeman who does the marshalling?

blocks.note: first meaning: a man from the Yard, Scotland Yard
second meaning: a railway worker who makes up trains in the sidings

explanation.walkthrough: Scotland Yard is the headquarters of London's Metropolitan Police; marshalling here is sorting railway wagons, not the US lawman.
explanation.definitionFit: A Yard man is a Scotland Yard detective, and a railway yardman shunts and arranges wagons in a marshalling yard.

clue.text: PM at Morecambe knew the road to Wigan pier

definitions.text: knew the road to Wigan pier

blocks.note: Eric Morecambe was the comedian of Morecambe and Wise
Tony Blair was the Prime Minister when the puzzle appeared

explanation.surface: A Prime Minister at the seaside town of Morecambe, knowing the way to Wigan.
explanation.walkthrough: Morecambe is a Lancashire resort, but here it is the comedian Eric Morecambe.
explanation.definitionFit: George Orwell's real name was this, and Orwell wrote The Road to Wigan Pier about poverty in northern England.

clue.text: Advice to girl if 'er boyfriend's shy? Turn down the light!

definitions.text: Advice to girl if 'er boyfriend's shy?

blocks.clueFragment: Advice to girl if 'er boyfriend's shy?
blocks.note: first meaning: said with a dropped h, the cheeky counsel to take him to bed
second meaning: to make dim

explanation.walkthrough: The dropped h in 'er tells you to read the answer the same way, as bed 'im. Turning down the light also suits the shy boyfriend.
explanation.definitionFit: To bedim is to make something dim or obscure, which is what lowering a lamp does.

clue.text: Take off your homburg and have a lozenge

indicators.note: to take off is to lift a part away, so a run of letters is lifted from the words

blocks.note: spans the end of your and the start of homburg

explanation.surface: Remove your hat and have a cough sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: A homburg is a felt hat with a dented crown. Lozenge suggests a cough sweet; here it is the diamond shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhomb, or rhombus, is a four-sided figure with equal sides, the diamond shape also called a lozenge.

clue.text: One person's mathematical unit

indicators.note: 's stands for has, so the words hold the answer within them

blocks.note: spans the end of one and the start of person

explanation.surface: A single person's own unit of measure.
explanation.definitionFit: The neper is a logarithmic unit for ratios, named after John Napier, used in mathematics and acoustics.

clue.text: The base and the elite to start making up?

blocks.note: a foundation is the base a building stands on
the cream is the best, the elite

explanation.surface: Society's lowest and highest classes beginning to reconcile.
explanation.walkthrough: Base and elite look like social classes and making up like reconciling; the setting is cosmetics.
explanation.definitionFit: Foundation is the cosmetic applied first to the face, so it is what one uses when beginning to put on make-up.

clue.text: What's gloomy about me - I can't concentrate

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: drear is a poetic word for dismal or gloomy
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asking what has got them down and why they cannot focus.
explanation.walkthrough: Drear is a literary form of dreary, rarely met outside poetry and crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A daydreamer drifts off and cannot keep their attention on the task, so the answer is spoken as a self-description.

clue.text: Nigel, the writer, takes some damask from the brocade

indicators.note: takes from means removes out of, so letters are lost

blocks.note: baldachin is a rich brocade of silk and gold
only some of damask: its first two letters

explanation.surface: A writer cutting a piece of damask from some brocade.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing DA from BALDACHIN leaves the surname of Nigel Balchin, author of The Small Back Room.
explanation.definitionFit: Nigel Balchin was a British novelist of the mid-twentieth century, so his surname answers the writer named Nigel.
